kurz: How the magic formula, the Piotroski score and the 200-day rule work in detail, and what is left of their results after data snooping, costs and German tax.

bloecke.md:
A rules-based approach replaces case-by-case decisions with a procedure that is fixed before the first purchase. A set of rules is complete only when it has three parts. The **universe** determines which securities are eligible at all, which industries are excluded and what minimum size applies. The **signal** specifies which ratios are ranked, and in what order. The **rebalancing rule** determines when to buy, when to sell and how often to review. If one of the three parts is missing, what remains is a collection of ratios that, when it counts, ends up being applied by gut feeling after all.

The three best-known sets of rules stand for three different ideas. Greenblatt's magic formula looks for cheap companies with a high return on capital. Within the cheap segment, Piotroski's F-score separates the stable companies from the financially weak ones. The 200-day rule calls for exiting the market as soon as the price falls below its own long-term average. Two of them are selection rules, the third is a timing rule. How robust the evidence is in each case depends on this distinction.

bloecke.titel: Test for a set of rules
bloecke.md: A procedure is a set of rules only if a stranger could rebuild it from the written description alone and would arrive at an identical portfolio. If a rule needs interpretation, room for discretion remains, even when ratios are used.

## Rules of the magic formula

Greenblatt creates two separate rankings across the entire universe and adds up the positions. The lowest combined rank comes first. Weightings, exceptions and the price-earnings ratio play no role.

bloecke.formel: Total rank = rank(EBIT / enterprise value) + rank(EBIT / (net working capital + net fixed assets))
bloecke.erklaerung: The first ratio (earnings yield) measures how cheap the company is relative to its enterprise value, that is, the market value of equity plus net financial debt. The second (return on capital) measures how well it uses the capital required for operations. Both measures are based on EBIT and total capital rather than on earnings per share. As a result, debt and the tax rate do not distort the comparison.
variablen: operating profit before interest and taxes
market capitalisation plus net financial debt
current assets minus non-interest-bearing current liabilities
property, plant and equipment after depreciation
bloecke.beispiel: Position 18 on earnings yield and position 150 on return on capital give a combined rank of 168. Such a security ranks behind one with positions 60 and 70 (sum 130). The formula therefore favours securities that do well on both ratios, even if they are not at the top of either.

schritte.text: The minimum market capitalisation is typically above $50 million. Financials, utilities and ADRs are excluded. For banks and insurers, “capital employed” is not a meaningful measure; for utilities, the return on capital is regulated.

schritte.titel: Create both rankings and add them up
schritte.text: The rankings are created separately by earnings yield and by return on capital, and then the positions are added up.
With fewer securities, the risk of individual holdings rises so sharply that the statistics behind the formula no longer apply.
Two to three positions are bought each month, so that the entire capital does not depend on a single reference date.
On its anniversary, each position is replaced by the security that is then ranked highest. Mathematically, this means 100% turnover a year.

bloecke.md: An independent analysis for 2003 to 2015 arrives at 11.4% a year compared with 8.7% for the S&P 500, with higher volatility. Up to mid-2007, the rule achieved around 26% a year against 18% for the index. From 2007 to 2010, the portfolio fell by as much as 57% (index: 55%), and after 2010 it lagged slightly behind the index at 12% against 13% a year. Greenblatt's own backtest figures from the book (1988 to 2004) are deliberately not quoted here, because they come from the author of the strategy and have not been independently verified.

bloecke.unter: Shown is the only independent analysis that could be verified for this lesson. The magic formula was 2.7 percentage points a year ahead, with higher volatility and a long weak phase from mid-2007.

bloecke.titel: Sale dates based on US tax law
bloecke.md: Greenblatt prescribes selling losers one week before the anniversary and winners one week after it. This rule serves solely to optimise tax in the United States, where the one-year period separates short-term from long-term capital gains. The German flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) has no holding period for shares. Investors in Germany who adopt this rule shift execution dates to no effect whatsoever and trade twice instead of once. Rules from other tax systems must be checked for their purpose before they are adopted.

## Piotroski's F-score with nine yes/no criteria

Piotroski designed the F-score as a filter within a value universe rather than as a stand-alone strategy. Many shares that look cheap on the ratios are cheap because the survival of the companies is at risk. The score comprises nine criteria, each worth one point. A score of 8 to 9 points is considered strong, 0 to 2 weak. Six of the nine criteria measure a change rather than a level. The direction in which a company is developing is harder to dress up than a figure on a reporting date.

bloecke.titel: The nine criteria of the F-score
kopf: What it is meant to test
zeilen: whether the company makes money at all
whether the business also brings in cash
return on capital vs. prior year
cash flow greater than net profit
no dilution because of a cash shortage
more revenue per euro of assets

bloecke.md: Four criteria concern profitability, three debt and liquidity, and two operating efficiency. The accrual test (operating cash flow greater than net profit) is the most valuable single point, because it targets accruals, where cosmetic adjustments to the accounts are easiest. The same logic underlies the Beneish M-score, which combines eight ratio indices into a suspicion of manipulation. Values above −1.78 are considered conspicuous there. The Altman Z-score assesses how close a company is to insolvency. Values above 2.99 are considered unremarkable, 1.81 to 2.99 a grey zone, and values below that indicate distress, that is, financial difficulty.

All three tools have industry-dependent reference values and a defined scope of application. The Altman Z-score is not intended for banks, insurers and property companies, and the Beneish M-score is expressly not intended for financial institutions. The F-score does not make sense for banks either, because the current ratio and the debt ratio mean something completely different there. If a score is ranked across industry boundaries, the result is a ranking of business models rather than of quality.

## The 200-day rule and its evidence

Under the rule, you are invested if the price on the review date is above the average of the last 200 trading days, and not otherwise. The review typically takes place once a month to limit the number of signals. Technically, a moving average is a low-pass filter, not a forecasting model. It smooths out short-term fluctuations (noise) and inevitably lags behind the price. Every signal therefore comes late. This delay results from the formula itself and cannot be remedied by better implementation.

The history of research shows how strongly the results depend on the testing method. In 1992, Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron found strong evidence for simple moving average and breakout rules in Dow data from 1897 to 1986. In 1999, Sullivan, Timmermann and White tested with a bootstrap across the entire universe of rules instead of only the one rule selected with hindsight. For 1897 to 1986 the results survived this correction, but in the ten years that followed (1987 to 1996) even the best rule no longer delivered a significant advantage. Bajgrowicz and Scaillet confirmed this in 2012 using false discovery methods. After correction for multiple testing and realistic transaction costs, practically nothing remains, and the rules that used to be successful are not persistent. The major survey by Park and Irwin counts 95 modern studies with 56 positive, 20 negative and 19 mixed results. The authors themselves note that most of these studies suffer from data snooping, rule selection after the fact and overly optimistic cost assumptions.

What a trend rule reliably changes is only the shape of the return distribution, not the return. There are fewer very deep slumps, but many small false signals in sideways markets. This trade-off can make sense, although in Germany it is taxable.

## Biases in backtests

Four errors make almost any backtest look too good, namely **overfitting** (parameters were fitted to the past), **look-ahead bias** (information used was not yet available at the time of trading, such as balance sheet data corrected later or index members added after the fact), **survivorship bias** (bankruptcies and delistings are missing from the data set) and costs that are set too low. In addition, there is the multiple testing problem. If enough variants are tested, one that looks good can be found even in pure random noise. Harvey, Liu and Zhu therefore call for a t-statistic above 3.0 for new signals instead of the usual 1.96. Hou, Xue and Zhang replicated 447 anomalies. Of these, 64% were already insignificant at t above 1.96 and 85% at t above 3.0, mainly because microcaps and equal weighting had inflated the original results.

The gap between backtest and reality can be measured. For 97 published predictors, McLean and Pontiff show that the return is 26% lower out of sample and 58% lower after publication. For 204 long-short anomalies, Chen and Velikov calculate that, after bid-ask spreads and the publication effect, the expected return averages 4 basis points a month, around 0.5% a year. Tradable products provide the strictest test. Before the launch of the associated ETF, smart beta indices showed around 3% excess return in the backtest, and −0.5 to −1% afterwards.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation, starting from an assumed backtest excess return of 6 percentage points. Deducted are the publication effect according to McLean/Pontiff, 0.3 percentage points of trading costs for one full turnover, and the tax hurdle from the next chart.

bloecke.md:
In the **walk-forward method**, optimisation is carried out on a rolling basis on one section of the data and tested on the next, untouched section. The protection is lost as soon as the same data are looked at repeatedly and the rules are readjusted. Out of sample then becomes in sample again.

The **deflated Sharpe ratio** corrects the Sharpe ratio for the number of variants tested and for returns that are not normally distributed. Without information on how many variants were tested, a Sharpe ratio from a backtest is not a reliable measure.

The **probability of backtest overfitting** estimates the probability that the configuration that was best in the test performs below average out of sample.

The cheapest check is to record the number of your own attempts before any result looks good. After 300 tested parameter combinations, a considerably stronger result is needed for the same significance than after a single test.

## Taxes and costs in Germany

All of these sets of rules require regular purchases and sales, and in Germany every trade costs twice, on the stock exchange and at the tax office. Realised price gains on shares are subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax plus the solidarity surcharge, an effective 26.375% excluding church tax. For equity ETFs, the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) reduces the effective burden to around 18.46%. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 (€2,000 for joint assessment) covers only the first few years for a set of rules with full annual turnover. Losses from share sales go into the separate share loss pot (Aktien-Verlusttopf) and can only be offset against gains on shares. In addition, the deduction of income-related expenses (Werbungskosten) is ruled out under the flat-rate withholding tax, so screening subscriptions, data feeds and software do not reduce the tax.

The lost deferral effect has a stronger impact than the tax rate. An investor who buys once and holds for thirty years pays tax once at the end, on the entire gain. Until then, the portion that is later paid over as tax also remains invested and continues to earn a return. With a complete turnover every year, this compounding on the tax portion is permanently lost.

bloecke.titel: Portfolio value with and without annual reallocation
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with €50,000, a 7% gross return and 26.375% flat-rate withholding tax, without the saver's allowance. Both curves show the value after sale and tax; after 30 years, they are €67,600 apart.

serien.name: buy once, pay tax at the end

bloecke.md: With a 7% gross return and 25 years, a set of rules with full annual turnover has to earn 8.11% gross to draw level after tax with a portfolio that is simply held. More than one percentage point of advantage is therefore needed, and order fees are not yet included in that.

A portfolio of 30 positions that are completely replaced once a year requires 60 orders a year. At an assumed fee of €4 per order, that comes to €240. For a portfolio of €50,000, this corresponds to 0.48% a year; for €15,000, it is already 1.6%, so the same rule is three times as expensive there. In addition, there is half the spread on each side, which is considerably wider for small caps and outside Xetra's core trading hours than for blue chips.

The fee assumption is uncertain in 2026. The EU ban on payment for order flow has applied to German brokers since 1 July 2026; since then, brokers have had to earn their revenue from order fees, spreads and interest margins. Before starting a trading-intensive set of rules, you should therefore check your own broker's current price list.

## Commitment to rules as protection against your own mistakes

The greater benefit of a set of rules usually lies in the fact that the decision for periods of stress has already been made, and less in any excess return. Morningstar's study “Mind the Gap” puts the gap between the return of funds and the return of their investors at 1.2 percentage points a year for the decade to the end of 2025 (9.9% against 8.7%). It arises solely from the timing and size of purchases and sales. The gap widens with volatility. In the calmest fifth of funds it is 0.4 percentage points, in the most volatile over 2.0, and for broad US large-cap funds it is practically zero. However, this finding is also disputed. In the Financial Analysts Journal in 2026, Fulkerson, Jordan, Riley and Yan argue that poor timing costs less than claimed.

A rule only protects you as long as it is followed. From mid-2007, the magic formula went through a weak phase lasting several years. An investor who “readjusts” in the third year is no longer following a set of rules and is in effect once again deciding by gut feeling, only with more effort. That is why every set of rules needs a stopping criterion formulated in advance that relates to the procedure and not to the latest return.

bloecke.titel: Put it in writing in advance
bloecke.md:
- For the universe, the exchanges and the minimum size are fixed, together with the excluded industries and the reasons for excluding them.
- For the signal, the ratio, the annual report and the reference date are fixed. The data source is part of this, otherwise look-ahead bias arises in everyday use too.
- The date is a fixed review day in the year or month, not “when I have time”.
- The position size is fixed in advance, equally weighted or according to a rule.
- The stopping criterion describes how to tell that the rule no longer works, as opposed to merely going through a weak phase. It relates to the procedure (e.g. data quality, tradability, cost situation) and not to the annual return.
- The log records every deviation with date and reason. Without a log, no honest evaluation is possible later, because deviations are easily forgotten or glossed over in hindsight.

mitnehmen: A set of rules consists of universe, signal and rebalancing rule. If one part is missing, decisions are once again made at discretion, despite the ratios.

The magic formula adds the ranks for EBIT/enterprise value and for EBIT relative to the capital required for operations. With six of its nine criteria, the Piotroski score measures changes rather than levels.
Trend rules such as the 200-day line mainly change the shape of the distribution, not the return. After correction for data snooping and costs, little of the excess return remains.
Published anomalies lose 26% of their original premium out of sample and 58% after publication. Backtest figures are therefore upper limits, not expected values.
In Germany, full annual turnover forfeits the tax deferral effect. With 7% gross and 25 years, 8.11% is then needed to draw level after tax.

begriffe.text: Set of rules devised by Joel Greenblatt. Shares are ranked separately by earnings yield (EBIT/enterprise value) and by return on capital, and the ranks are then added up. The portfolio holds 20 to 30 securities with complete annual turnover, excluding financials and utilities.

Score from 0 to 9 based on nine yes/no criteria on profitability, debt and efficiency, mostly measured as the change from the previous year. It is intended as a filter within a value universe, not as a stand-alone strategy.
Error in a backtest in which information is used that was not yet available at the simulated time of trading, such as balance sheet data corrected later or index members added after the fact.

Searching through many variants of rules and parameters until one looks good. Because the number of attempts is ignored, random noise appears to be a finding. Higher t-hurdles and the deflated Sharpe ratio serve as remedies.

Advantage of a portfolio that is not sold. As long as no gain is realised, the tax portion that falls due later also remains invested and earns a return. Every realisation ends this effect for the amount concerned.
